title: Require adversarial red-teaming and a tested kill switch before deploying a publicly-facing AI system that learns from live input
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on the Microsoft Tay chatbot incident. Not a documented decision of any specific organization.

history.note: Initial Phase 2A seed content, part of the Foundational Twenty.

Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources). decision_statement: Before deploying a publicly-facing AI system that adapts its behaviour from live user input, the organization must conduct adversarial red-teaming specifically targeting coordinated manipulation attempts, and must have a tested kill-switch/rollback mechanism capable of disabling the system within minutes of detecting harmful output at scale.
decision_context: Motivated by Microsoft's Tay chatbot, which was manipulated into posting offensive content within hours of launch by coordinated trolling exploiting its live-learning design, and was only disabled after the harm had already become public.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Public-Facing AI Systems Governance Board
alternatives_considered: Rely on post-launch monitoring alone without pre-launch adversarial testing.
Treat a kill-switch as a manual, undocumented ad hoc response rather than a tested, rehearsed procedure.

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this incident.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.
A tested kill-switch and rollback plan is the concrete implementation of this control's post-deployment monitoring requirement.
Compliance must be demonstrated by a documented red-team test report.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking how quickly a harmful public-facing AI system could actually be disabled.
